title: An Overview of Long-Run Economic Growth

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Welcome back. Today we are on long-run economic growth: how living standards rise over decades and centuries. Let's start with a guessing game.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Okay. I'll describe a country, and you tell me which one it is. A baby born there can expect to live less than 50 years. 1 baby in 10 dies before its first birthday. More than 90 percent of homes have no electricity, no fridge, no phone and no car.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That sounds like one of the poorest countries in the world today.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Good guess, but no. It's the United States, more than a hundred years ago, around 1900. Growth changed that country completely. But many other countries did not have that growth.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So here is today's question. Why are some countries so much richer than others, and how do we read growth from the data?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: By the end of this episode, you'll be able to do three things. First, describe how recent lasting growth is, and explain how it opened huge gaps between countries. Second, use two simple tools. The Rule of 70 tells you how long an income takes to double. The growth rules split total growth into growth per person and population growth. Third, explain why growing a little faster each year, kept up for decades, separates rich countries from poor ones.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And we'll follow the chapter's mind map part by part?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Yes. The map has three parts, or branches. Part one gives the long-run facts. Part two builds the mathematics of growth. Part three compares countries and people. Each part has a few leaves, small topics we take in order.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Part one of the map: The long-run facts. The first leaf says sustained growth is recent. What do we measure, and what does sustained mean?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: We measure living standards with GDP per person. GDP, or gross domestic product, is the value of all the final goods and services a country produces in a year. Final means bought by the people who use them, like bread, not the flour inside it. Divide GDP by the number of people, and you get average income per person. Sustained growth means that this income rises year after year, for a long time.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Okay. Then over the last 2,000 years, my guess is that income per person grew slowly and steadily the whole time.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: That's what most people guess, but it's wrong. For almost all of history, income per person stayed close to the level where people can barely survive. Then, only in the last two or three centuries, it climbed very fast. People call this shape a hockey stick: a long flat handle, then a sharp turn upward at the end.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So for most of history, people lived about as well as their great-grandparents.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Exactly. Our imaginary island country, Islandia, has the same story. For most of its history, income per person on the island barely changed. Then it began to rise a little every year, and it has kept rising ever since.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: How big is the rise in a real country?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Take the United Kingdom. In 2022, its income per person was 33 times its level in the year 1, about 2,000 years ago.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And when did most of that rise happen?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Almost all of it came after 1800. Why it started then is still debated, and Chapter 6 comes back to it. But we know it did not start everywhere at once. It came first to the United Kingdom and the United States, later to Japan and Argentina, and to China only in recent decades. In Ghana, the rise has been much smaller.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That brings us to the next leaf: the Great Divergence. Divergence means moving apart, right?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Right. Before 1700, the richest countries were probably at most 2 or 3 times as rich as the poorest. Then growth started at different times in different places. Each early starter kept growing, so small gaps became huge ones.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: How huge?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: In 2022, income per person in Ghana was about one fourteenth of the U.S. level. In other words, the average American was about 14 times as rich as the average person in Ghana. This widening of the gaps is what economists call the Great Divergence.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Next leaf: U.S. GDP per person since 1870. How much richer is an American today?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: In 1870, GDP per person in the United States was 4,634 dollars a year. Both numbers I'll give you use the same prices, so they compare what people could really buy.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And in 2022?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: 77,942 dollars. That's almost 17 times as much. And over time, the yearly rise in dollars kept getting bigger.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So U.S. growth has been speeding up.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: A lot of students think that, but not really. The percentage rise stays roughly the same, around 2 percent a year. 2 percent of a large income is simply more dollars than 2 percent of a small income.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So in part one we saw that lasting growth is new in history. It began at different times in different places, and that turned small gaps into huge ones. And in the U.S., a steady rate of about 2 percent a year made income almost 17 times as large since 1870.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Yes. Next branch: the mathematics that turns a small rate into such a big change.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Part two of the map: The mathematics of growth. The first leaf is the constant growth rule, the equation for steady growth. Let's start simple. What is a growth rate?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: A growth rate is a percentage change: how much something changed in a year, divided by where it started. Let's go back to Islandia. Today each islander earns 6 units of the goods the island makes, and income grows by 2 percent a year.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So what happens in the first year?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Income gains 2 percent of 6, which is 0.12. So after one year, income is 6.12.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And the year after?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Again 2 percent, but now of 6.12, so the gain is a little bigger. Each year, you multiply income by 1.02, which is one plus the growth rate. Do that once for each year, and you have the constant growth rule.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Let me guess where Islandia is after a century. The gain grows only a tiny bit each year, so let's say 0.12 a year. A century adds about 12. My guess is 18.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: That's the natural guess, but it's far too low. 18 is what you get if every year adds the same amount. With a constant growth rate, each year's gain is taken of a bigger income, because last year's gain is now part of it. Economists call this compounding. After 100 years, Islandia's income is 43.5 units.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: 43.5! That's more than seven times where it started.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Right. On an ordinary chart, that path bends upward more and more steeply. Next leaf: the ratio scale, another way to draw growth. On an ordinary chart, each equal step up adds the same amount: one, two, three, four. On a ratio scale, each equal step multiplies by the same amount: one, two, four, eight.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So on a ratio scale, Islandia's income still curves upward?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: No, it becomes a straight line. Under steady growth, income doubles again and again, at regular intervals. So it climbs one equal step in each interval. And a steeper line means faster growth.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And how long is each interval? Is that the next leaf, the Rule of 70?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Yes. Divide 70 by the growth rate, in percent. For Islandia, 70 divided by 2 gives 35 years. That's how long its income takes to double.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Why 70, and not some other number?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: At 1 percent a year, doubling takes almost exactly 70 years. Without compounding, it would take 100 years, but each year's gain also grows. If you grow twice as fast, doubling takes half as long.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Next leaf: the U.S. since 1870, about 2 percent a year. What does that mean?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Something remarkable. On a ratio scale, U.S. income since 1870 stays close to a straight line, with growth of about 2 percent a year, for more than 150 years.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Even through wars and the Great Depression, the deep economic crisis of the early 1930s?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Yes. The Great Depression and World War Two cause large swings, but the path comes back close to the same line. Look closely, and growth was a little slower before 1929 and a little faster in the decades after 1950. The exact average since 1870 is 1.88 percent a year.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Still on this leaf: where does an exact number like 1.88 come from, when the data go up and down?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: From the average growth rate. You use only the first value and the last value. You ask: what one steady yearly rate would take you from the first to the last in the same number of years? You can't just divide the total rise by the number of years, because growth compounds. Take Islandia's century. Its income went from 6 to 43.5, so it became about 7.2 times as large.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And then?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Then ask: what number, multiplied by itself 100 times, gives 7.2? The answer is 1.02. Take away the one that stands for the starting income, and 2 percent a year is left.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Islandia has good years and bad years too. Say, just for this example, a good year raises income by 20 percent, and then a bad year cuts it by 20 percent. On average that's zero, so islanders are back where they started.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Let's test it with simple numbers. Start at 100. A 20 percent rise takes you to 120.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And the 20 percent fall takes me back to 100.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: That's a common mistake. The fall hits a bigger income than the rise did. 20 percent of 120 is 24, so you end at 96.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So islanders end 4 percent poorer. What's the average growth rate, then?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Use the same method. It gives about minus 2 percent a year, not zero. A 2 percent fall, two years in a row, also takes 100 to about 96.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Last leaf of this part: growth rules. What are they?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: When you multiply two things, their growth rates add. When you divide one thing by another, their growth rates subtract. Total GDP is GDP per person times the number of people. It grows for two reasons at once: each person produces more, and there are more people. So total GDP grows at about the sum of those two growth rates.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Can we check it with the U.S.?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Since 1870, U.S. GDP per person grew 1.88 percent a year. The population grew 1.39 percent a year.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So total GDP grew about 3.3 percent a year, the sum.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Very close. The data say 3.29 percent a year. The rule is not exact, because each year's growth compounds a little, but for small rates the gap is tiny.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And the rule for dividing?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Income per person is total GDP divided by the number of people. So its growth rate is GDP growth minus population growth. Take Niger, one of the poorest countries in the world. Since 1950, its GDP grew 2.9 percent a year, but its population grew 2.8 percent a year. So income per person barely changed, even though GDP grew fast.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So in part two we built a toolkit for reading growth. Steady growth compounds, and 70 divided by the growth rate gives the doubling time. On a ratio scale, it's a straight line, like U.S. income at about 2 percent a year. The first and last values give the average rate. And growth rates add when we multiply and subtract when we divide.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Right. Next branch: what these tools show when countries grow at different rates.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Part three of the map: Across countries and people. The first leaf is catch-up. What does that mean?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Catch-up means a poorer country grows faster than a richer one, so it closes part of the gap. Economists also call it convergence. South Korea is a famous example. In 1950, its income per person was only 7 percent of the U.S. level.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And by now?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: By 2022, it was 71 percent. Korea grew so much faster than the United States that it closed most of the gap. Japan did something similar after World War Two.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So poor countries naturally grow faster. Give them time, and they all catch up.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Look at Argentina. It grew well until about 1980, then slowly, and it fell behind. So no: catch-up happens, but not automatically, and not everywhere. And since 1960, poor countries as a group did not grow faster than rich ones on average.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Did some countries actually get poorer?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Yes, a few, like the Democratic Republic of the Congo. But since 2000, many poor countries have grown as fast as rich ones, or faster.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Next leaf: Singapore, and how small gaps in growth compound. What counts as a small gap here?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Here the gap is a difference in growth rates, not in income. Since 1960, most countries grew between 1 and 3 percent a year.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Can such small differences really matter that much?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Over decades, they can. Look at Singapore. It grew 5.9 percent a year, several percentage points faster than most countries. A percentage point is the step from 2 percent a year to 3 percent a year. Singapore's income became about 36 times as large.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: 36 times! How does 5.9 percent turn into that?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Let's build that number step by step. First, the doubling time. 70 divided by 5.9 is about 12.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So Singapore's income doubled about every 12 years. How many doublings is that?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: The data cover 63 years. Five doublings take five times 12 years, which is 60 years. So there's time for a bit more than five doublings.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And what do five doublings give?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Each doubling multiplies income by 2. After two doublings, income is 4 times as large. After three, 8 times.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Then 16 times after four doublings, and 32 times after five.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Exactly. The few extra years add a little more. The exact figure in the data is 36 times, so the shortcut gets us close. In Singapore, young adults today are many times richer than their grandparents were at the same age. In Madagascar, people are slightly poorer. That's the difference that a few percentage points of growth a year can make.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Next leaf: counting people, and the share below the poverty line. Haven't we been counting people all along?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Not quite. So far, each country counted once. China, with more than a billion people, counted the same as a tiny country. Now every person counts equally. We draw a very low poverty line: an average income of about 3,400 dollars a year per person. Then we ask what share of the world's people live in countries below it.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Poverty is always in the news. So my guess is that the share of poor people has barely fallen.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: The data show the opposite. In 1960, 69 percent of the world's people lived below that line.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And in 2019?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Only 8.5 percent. The fall was slow until about 1990, and very fast after that. That's mostly China and India. Together they are home to more than a third of the world's people, and their fast growth moved hundreds of millions above the line.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Is there a problem with this way of counting?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: One caution. It uses each country's average income, so it ignores inequality inside countries. Surveys of households tell the same broad story, though: a large fall in poverty since 1990.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Last leaf: can policy start growth, and at what cost?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: The economist Robert Lucas asked a famous question about India. Is there something its government could do to make India grow like the fastest growers? If so, what exactly?

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So what does the evidence say?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Growth take-offs, when growth speeds up by at least two percentage points for eight years or more, are common. Keeping them going for decades is rare.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So what did the fast growers do?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: They usually invested a lot, opened up to trade and kept their economies stable. Rules that protect property and contracts, what economists call institutions, matter in the long run. But the question is still debated. Most take-offs follow no clear change in policy, so luck plays a role. And what works in one country often fails in another.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And the cost? More growth means more pollution, doesn't it?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Growth does have costs: pollution, using up natural resources, and climate change. Local pollution often gets worse early in development and then better as incomes rise. London's smog, a thick fog of smoke, was deadly for many decades. Today London's air is far cleaner.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So pollution goes away by itself as countries get richer?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Not by itself. The cleaner air came from rules and regulation. And the gases that warm the planet harm everyone, not only the country that produces them. Still, most economists who study these costs think the benefits of growth are larger. In the poorest countries, the main problem is too little growth, not too much.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So in part three we saw that a few extra percentage points of growth, kept up for decades, made South Korea and Singapore rich, while others fell behind. Counting people, poverty fell sharply. And policy can help, but no one has a plan that works everywhere.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Yes. Let's sum up.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Let's go back to our three goals. First, how new is lasting growth, and why are the gaps so big?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Lasting growth began only two or three centuries ago. It started at different times in different places, and the early starters kept growing. So gaps of 2 or 3 times became gaps like the 14 times between the United States and Ghana.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Second, the tools. An income that grows 2 percent a year doubles in about 35 years, by the Rule of 70. And total growth is growth per person plus population growth.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Yes. So when GDP grows only as fast as the population, people get no richer.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Third, rich versus poor.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: South Korea and Singapore grew a few percentage points faster than most countries, for decades, and that made them rich. So here is the big message. Lasting growth is new in history, and it spread unevenly. And it compounds, so a few percentage points of growth a year, kept up for decades, is what separates rich countries from poor ones.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Here's a question to think about. A neighboring island is half as rich as Islandia today. Islandia keeps growing at 2 percent a year, and the neighbor grows at 3 percent a year. About how long until the neighbor catches up, and why?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Pause the episode and think about it for a moment.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Okay, we're back. What's the answer?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: About 70 years. Use the rule for dividing. The neighbor's income divided by Islandia's grows at 3 minus 2, so at 1 percent a year.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And the neighbor catches up when that ratio has doubled, from one half to one.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Exactly. At 1 percent a year, doubling takes about 70 years. That's two or three generations. And if both islands grew at the same rate, the neighbor would never catch up.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Where can students try all this themselves?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Open the chapter's Colab notebook to rebuild every number from the data. The Model Apps let you move a growth-rate slider and watch the doubling time change, with no code. The Data Apps let you add any country to the charts.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And next time?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: In Chapter 4, we build a first model to explain these gaps. We ask: why are some countries so much richer than others: more machines, or better use of them?

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That's it for today. Thanks for listening, and see you next time.
